answer: Each dawn the warden reads the water level on the gauge staff and writes the figure in the river book, and the gauge board is repainted once a year so no mark may be moved in secret. A nadir reading taken at noon fails the staff: at the umber of the gauge the water must stand where the dawn reading put it, and a noon reading hides the night's fall. Faking the gauge means bribing the warden, repainting the board and paying 8,200, while the haven figure in the river book is checked against the mills downstream, so a reading that was never taken is exposed by the first dry wheel.
